item.title: RAIN: Agentic Proof Generation for Rocq-based Software Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.30759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive theorem provers can provide strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing the proofs remains a challenging and labor-intensive task. Inspired by the recent progress of modern coding agents, we present RAIN, a lightweight proof-specialized agent for Rocq proof generation. RAIN augments an LLM with proof engineering capabilities, including repository exploration, iterative refinement, and checker feedback. This design allows the agent to retrieve lemmas autonomously, revise complete proof scripts instead of isolated tactics, and iteratively refine its proof strategy using enriched proof-state information. Evaluated on a subset from CoqStoq, RAIN shows substantial improvements over the existing baselines, achieving over 90% prove success rate with at least 24.7% improvements. We also compare with general-purpose coding agents, the results show that RAIN maintains comparable prove success rate but with significant lower cost.
item.dc:creator: Jinyi Zhou, Zenan Li, Yuan Yao, Jun Ma, Taolue Chen, Xiaoxing Ma

item.title: Global Convergence of Detailed Balanced Mass Action Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.30808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a self-contained proof that, for a finite detailed balanced mass-action system with positive rate constants, each positive stoichiometric compatibility class contains exactly one positive equilibrium and every positive trajectory converges to it, together with a Lean 4 formalization of the complete argument from persistence to convergence. Boundedness and persistence come from the barrier argument of OpenAI (2026) for weakly reversible systems: an arbitrary-tolerance affine approximation yields a finite-minimum barrier whose superlevel sets confine trajectories and give one logarithmic bound for all solutions from a given initial state. The Horn-Jackson dissipation identity identifies the positive equilibria as an exponential family with parameters in the orthogonal complement of the stoichiometric subspace, which gives uniqueness in each class. A bounded-speed descent argument replaces LaSalle's invariance principle; it uses neither uniqueness of solutions nor continuous dependence on initial data, and it places every cluster point in that family. The route given here is direct and elementary, and its main theorem is checked by the Lean kernel against explicit definitions. The proofs, the Lean development, and the manuscript were produced in ClawsGO Science, an agent harness that packages a complete research environment: Claude Opus 5.5 made the research decisions, GPT 6 Astra carried them out, and the Lean kernel checked every formal step.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Lv (BitMiracle AI Lab), Chengjin Ni (BitMiracle AI Lab), Manqin Wang (BitMiracle AI Lab), Shenli He (BitMiracle AI Lab)

item.title: Notation3: Graph Terms for RDF
item.description: arXiv:2610.31266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Notation3 Logic was introduced as an extension of RDF allowing the user to express rules on top of triples and to make statements about graphs. The original proposal of the logic only came with an informal specification of its semantics which has been refined later on. While this refinement clarified the meaning of rules and implicitly quantified variables, it left the meaning of graphs used as terms - so-called graph terms - open. In this paper we aim to close this gap. We discuss in detail, how graph terms are used in Notation3, which formal requirements they need to meet, and provide examples to illustrate the difficulties when defining their semantics. We then introduce an abstract syntax for the logic and define its semantics in two steps: similarly to RDF's simple interpretations, we define interpretations and basic entailment for Notation3 which covers plain RDF triples but also triples containing graph terms. N3-entailment is then an extension of basic entailment which assigns meaning to the different special predicates of the logic like for example the implication symbol. N3-entailment is defined in a way that it can be extended whenever a new predicate is added to the logic. As Notation3 Logic is currently under development, we expect many predicates to be added. Our research provides and important step towards the full standardisation of the logic.
item.dc:creator: D\"orthe Arndt, Pierre-Antoine Champin

item.title: Agentic Verified Optimization of Real-World Software
item.description: arXiv:2610.30188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Program optimization aims to improve performance while preserving behavior. Coding agents can already make programs faster by changing algorithms, data structures, and execution strategies. However, existing equivalence checks mostly rely on tests, which agents have been shown to exploit, passing the tests without preserving the intended behavior. We propose agentic verified optimization, in which an agent produces a faster implementation together with a machine-checked proof of equivalence to the existing one. Because the existing implementation serves as the specification, the task avoids the specification-writing bottleneck of verified code generation, and recent advances in theorem proving make the proofs attainable. We formulate the task at the function and repository levels in Lean 4, where programs can be both executed and reasoned about. Few real-world applications are written in Lean, so we develop Aqueduct, an agentic framework that migrates C, C++, Go, and Rust programs into native Lean, validates each port by differential testing against its original. On the 189 reference implementations in Verina, agents produce faster proved rewrites for 156, including algorithmic changes such as replacing exponential recursion with dynamic programming. On 17 migrated applications, their 92 proved rewrites speed up 47 of 51 application scenarios. These application-level gains are smaller than the function-level ones, making the choice of functions to optimize an important problem. Current agents can thus already carry out verified optimization on both standalone functions and applications migrated from real programs. We discuss the remaining challenges and the steps toward verified optimization in production.
item.dc:creator: Zhe Ye, Udaya Ghai, Zhizhen Qin, Dawn Song, Soonho Kong

item.title: TrustedCode: Evaluating Large Language Models for Developing Trusted Code through Automated Program Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.30432v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent reports, such as "Who is using AI to code?", indicate that approximately 30\% of Python code contributions to GitHub are AI-generated. Given the inherent unreliability of this code, formal verification emerges as a promising approach to establish trust in software correctness. Although leveraging large language models (LLMs) for formal verification has garnered increasing attention, practical adoption remains limited due to the challenges in writing formal specifications and verifying program correctness against them. Existing tools predominantly support verification for languages such as Java and C, with minimal support for Python. We present TrustedCode, an automated framework for verifying AI-generated Python code. TrustedCode uses LLMs to (i) type-check Python code, (ii) translate it into WhyML via the Why3 framework, and (iii) verify it against formal specifications using Why3 back-end automated theorem provers. Our method integrates chain-of-thought prompting through LangGraph to identify and address LLM limitations in specification generation and proving the specified programs. To evaluate TrustedCode, we conducted experiments on ten Python programs of varying complexity. Our analysis reveals that 50\% of the observed errors stem from domain knowledge gaps, 30\% from syntactic inaccuracies, and the remaining 20\% from semantic and type-related issues. These findings underscore the importance of targeted improvements in LLM-guided formal verification workflows for Python. TrustedCode is an open source tool available at: \href{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}. The video demonstration is available at: \href{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Danial, Muhammad Taimoor Khan

item.title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
item.description: arXiv:2610.30645v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.
item.dc:creator: Ruixuan Deng, Zhengfeng Ji, Jiayu Zhang, Li Zhou

item.title: On U_c-admitting spaces and U_c-completions of T_0 spaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.30967v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new class of spaces, termed U_c-admitting spaces, and investigate their relationships with U_s-admitting spaces and well-filtered spaces. Adopting the perspective of H-sobriety, we show that every U_c-admitting space is H-sober, so that U_c-admitting spaces arise as a special case of H-sober spaces. Consequently, the category U_c-Sob of U_c-admitting spaces and continuous maps is complete and forms a reflective subcategory of Top_0. In addition, we prove that a T_0 space X is U_c-admitting if and only if its Smyth power space is U_c-admitting. Finally, we present the standard U_c-completion of an arbitrary T_0 space.
item.dc:creator: Kangming Lu, Qingguo Li, Shengwen Wang, Rongqi Xiao

item.title: A declarative approach to specifying Paxos using three-valued modal fixpoint logic
item.description: arXiv:2502.00892v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Three-valued Fixpoint Quorum Logic, or 3muQL for short; a three-valued modal fixed-point logic designed for declaratively specifying and reasoning about distributed algorithms, such as the Paxos consensus algorithm. Our methodology represents a distributed algorithm as a logical theory, enabling correctness properties to be derived directly within the framework -- or revealing logical errors in the algorithm's design when they exist. 3muQL adopts a declarative approach, specifying the overall logic of computation without prescribing control flow. Notably, message-passing and state-transitions are not explicitly modelled, and notions of 'quorum' are abstracted from concrete thresholds to abstract modal operators. This distinguishes our framework from approaches like TLA+. The logical abstraction emphasises the essence of distributed algorithms, offering a novel perspective on their specification and reasoning. We define the syntax and semantics of 3muQL, explore its theoretical properties, and demonstrate its applicability through a detailed treatment of the Paxos consensus algorithm. By presenting Paxos as a logical theory and deriving its standard correctness properties, we showcase the framework's capacity to handle non-trivial distributed systems. We envision 3muQL as a versatile tool for specifying and reasoning about distributed algorithms. The Paxos example highlights the framework's ability to capture intricate details, offering a new lens through which distributed algorithms can be specified, studied, and checked. The ideas we present are easily implemented, and to demonstrate this we have implemented a freely-available proof-of- concept 3muQL model-checker, as an effective prototyping tool.
item.dc:creator: Murdoch J. Gabbay, Luca Zanolini

item.title: Ohana trees, linear approximation and multi-types for the $\lambda$I-calculus: No variable gets left behind or forgotten!
item.description: arXiv:2505.06193v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Although the $\lambda$I-calculus is a natural fragment of the $\lambda$-calculus, obtained by forbidding the erasure of arguments, its equational theories did not receive much attention. The reason is that all proper denotational models studied in the literature equate all non-normalizable $\lambda$I-terms, whence the associated theory is not very informative. The goal of this paper is to introduce a previously unknown theory of the $\lambda$I-calculus, induced by a notion of evaluation trees that we call "Ohana trees". The Ohana tree of a $\lambda$I-term is an annotated version of its B\"ohm tree, remembering all free variables that are hidden within its meaningless subtrees, or pushed into infinity along its infinite branches. We develop the associated theories of program approximation: the first approach -- more classic -- is based on finite trees and continuity, the second adapts Ehrhard and Regnier's Taylor expansion. We then prove a Commutation Theorem stating that the normal form of the Taylor expansion of a $\lambda$I-term coincides with the Taylor expansion of its Ohana tree. As a corollary, we obtain that the equality induced by Ohana trees is compatible with abstraction and application. Subsequently, we introduce a denotational model designed to capture the equality induced by Ohana trees. Although presented as a non-idempotent type system, our model is based on a suitably modified version of the relational semantics of the $\lambda$-calculus, which is known to yield proper models of the $\lambda$I-calculus when restricted to non-empty finite multisets. item.title: A simple formalization of alpha-equivalence
item.description: arXiv:2507.10181v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While teaching untyped $\lambda$-calculus to undergraduate students, we were wondering why $\alpha$-equivalence is not directly inductively defined. In this paper, we demonstrate that this is indeed feasible. Specifically, we provide a grounded, inductive definition for $\alpha$-equivalence and show that it conforms to the specification provided in the literature. The work presented in this paper is fully formalized in the Rocq Prover.
item.dc:creator: Kalmer Apinis, Danel Ahman

item.title: Cut elimination for the alternation-free modal mu-calculus
item.description: arXiv:2510.11293v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a syntactic cut-elimination procedure for the alternation-free fragment of the modal mu-calculus. Cut reduction is carried out within a cyclic proof system, where proofs are finitely branching but may be non-wellfounded. The structure of such proofs is exploited to directly transform a cyclic proof with cuts into a cut-free one, without detouring through other logics or relying on intermediate machinery for regularisation. Novel ingredients include the use of multicuts and results from the theory of well-quasi-orders, the later used in the termination argument.
item.dc:creator: Bahareh Afshari, Johannes Kloibhofer

item.title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
item.description: arXiv:2610.20573v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract-Verify-Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted-error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at https://github.com/annamei1/FLMF-Ch7ErrFunc-Release.git.
item.dc:creator: Anna Mei, Michael R. Douglas

item.title: Diophantine Equations over $\mathbb Z$: Universal Bounds and Parallel Formalization
item.description:
arXiv:2506.20909v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper explores multiple closely related themes: bounding the complexity of Diophantine equations over the integers and developing mathematical proofs in parallel with formal theorem provers. Hilbert's Tenth Problem (H10) asks about the decidability of Diophantine equations and has been answered negatively by Davis, Putnam, Robinson and Matiyasevich. It is natural to ask for which subclasses of Diophantine equations H10 remains undecidable. Such subclasses can be defined in terms of universal pairs: bounds on the number of variables $
u$ and degree $\delta$ such that all Diophantine equations can be rewritten in at most this complexity. Our work develops explicit universal pairs $(
u, \delta)$ for integer unknowns, focused on reducing the number of unknowns to $
u = 11$. This achieves new bounds that cannot be obtained by naive translations from known results over $\mathbb{N}$. In parallel, we have conducted a formal verification of our results using the proof assistant Isabelle. While formal proof verification has traditionally been applied a posteriori to known results, this project integrates formalization into the discovery and development process. In a final section, we describe key insights gained from this approach and its implications for mathematical practice. Our work contributes both to the study of Diophantine equations and to the broader question of how mathematics is conducted in the 21st century.
item.dc:creator: Jonas Bayer, Marco David, Malte Hassler, Yuri Matiyasevich, Dierk Schleicher

item.title: Logics vs doctrines, a mirror symmetry
item.description: arXiv:2610.29771v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the relationship between doctrines, encoding 2-categories of theories in predicate logic, and fragments of geometric logic, defined through Kan injectivity in the 2-category of topoi. After a brief historical account of the notion of doctrine, we propose our working definition. Our main result then establishes a Galois connection between doctrines and subgeometric logics. This connection suggests a mirror symmetry between the world of doctrines and the world of logics, in which constructions and results on either side admit counterparts on the other. We develop this symmetry through constructions of syntactic categories and classifying topoi in both settings, recovering the familiar examples from categorical logic. We prove paired Diaconescu-type theorems and give symmetric universal characterisations of the two closure operators induced by the Galois connection. Finally, we show that passing from a doctrine to its closure induces a reflection between the corresponding 2-categories of algebras, and we relate this reflection to conceptual completeness.
item.dc:creator: Ivan Di Liberti, Umberto Tarantino, Lingyuan Ye
